newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to focus on Western Hemisphere in second term.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to focus on Western Hemisphere in second term.

text.p: President Bill Clinton will focus on strengthening democracy and promoting trade with Latin America and Caribbean nations during his second term, a senior State Department official said on Wednesday.
"The next 12 months will see an intense focus on regional issues by the president," Assistant Secretary of State Jeffrey Davidow said at a hearing of the House Western Hemisphere Subcommittee.

Clinton is scheduled to go to Mexico in April, visit five Latin American and Caribbean countries in May and attend the second Summit of the Americas in Chile in March, 1998. He recently hosted a visit by Chilean President Eduardo Frei.
"This high level of activity is indicative of the importance the administration gives to relations with the nations of our hemisphere," Davidow said.
He said Clinton's policy goals for the region were to promote free trade, strengthen democracy, fight drug trafficking and encourage economic development and poverty alleviation programmes.

"While democracy is now commonplace in Latin America and the Caribbean, we should not be complacent and assume it always will be. If democratic institutions are weak, disfunctional or corrupt, the hard-earned gains of the last decade could be erased," Davidow said.
He said U.S. efforts to support democracy in the region included programmes for judicial reforms and fair elections and to support human rights groups and fight corruption.

Davidow said the United States was committed to establishing a Free Trade Area of the Americas by the year 2005, as set by the 1994 Summit of the Americas. But he said the administration needed expanded trade negotiation authority from Congress.

Davidow defended Clinton's decision to recertify Mexico as a full partner in the war against drugs, saying, "Full certification is the best means to achieve maximum success against the flow of drugs into our country."
The U.S. House of Representatives has voted to reverse Clinton's action in 90 days unless Mexico improves its anti-drug cooperation, and the Senate may do so as well.

But Davidow said that would be a mistake: "Economically, the likely effect of any successful action to overturn the president's decision would be higher Mexican interest rates and lower growth prospects."
But he said tough economic sanctions remained the best way to promote democracy in Cuba, along with increased contacts between Cubans and U.S. groups.
